beads.title: Closed loop: measure unattended quality against turn count
beads.body: The deliverable is the CURVE, not the artifacts. docs/CLOSED-LOOP.md is the design record; this graph is its execution. A programme that cannot report 'this does not work' is not an experiment — every phase below carries a stop-if.

beads.title: Ticket graph: append-only ledger with derived scheduling
beads.body: JSONL, last-record-per-id wins, so two branches merge by concatenation. Blocked-ness is derived, never stored. dead-end is a first-class kind: the memory that stops turn 30 redoing turn 4.

beads.title: Contagion firewall: assert a loop commit's blast radius
beads.body: CLOSED-LOOP.md 7 required this before the first autonomous commit. 140 of 151 workflows are push-triggered; the check asserts the set a loop commit can wake is a subset of the set it declares. Fails towards yes.

beads.title: loop.mino.mobi — the public viewing surface for the graph
beads.body: The apparatus is operator content, so it lives on mino.mobi. The artifacts a loop builds are agent-generated and belong on minomobi.com. CLOSED-LOOP.md 6.1.

beads.title: Phase 1 — pilot: one artifact, 10 turns, judge stubbed as a human-scored rubric
beads.body: STOP-IF: turns 5-10 are not visibly better than 1-4. That is a result, and the programme stops. The pilot exists to be cheap enough that a negative result is affordable. Second job: replace the cost estimate in CLOSED-LOOP.md 10, which is flagged there as the weakest number in the document.

beads.title: Phase 2 — the judge: probes + rubric + adversarial, calibrated against the pilot's human scores
beads.body: STOP-IF: the judge disagrees with people. There is no evaluation function anywhere in this repo today (CLOSED-LOOP.md 3, checked not assumed). A closed loop without a judge is a random walk with a commit log. Disagreement between the three signals is itself data.

beads.title: Phase 3 — seed the graph from the 59 BRIEF.md plan sections and the refusal reports
beads.body:
There is a second backlog nobody is reading: every lab site's BRIEF.md ends with a section its agent wrote FOR ITS SUCCESSOR. 59 of them, inert since the day each was written. That is a bead in all but name — state, ordering, a handoff — sitting as unqueryable prose on a published page.

DROPPED: Superseded by the greenfield decision (lp-DECISION below). The 59 BRIEF.md plan sections are community submissions — other people's projects, requested in their own threads. Spending 20-40 unattended turns iterating on them is a bad fit whoever benefits, and the backlog being convenient is not a reason. Greenfield replaces this phase: the operator writes a spec and a planner decomposes it.

beads.title: Phase 4 — the run: budgeted, instrumented, on its own surface
beads.body: 3-5 artifacts x 20-40 turns, not 100 x 1. Depth over breadth: the curve only exists along the turn axis, and breadth is the thing we already know. Stop conditions all three required.

beads.title: Phase 5 — publish the curve
beads.body: The deliverable. Most agent-loop demonstrations show you a terminal and ask you to be impressed; a measured quality-against-duration curve is a genuinely unusual public artifact.

beads.title: Flip .github/loop/config.json enabled to true
beads.body: The master switch, off by design. Same shape as ANNOUNCE in bsky-hello.yml and BOT_ENABLED in the factory: the expensive, irreversible half starts with a diff someone signed. Do not flip before Phase 1 has run attended at least once.

beads.title: Set CRON_GITHUB_PAT so the cron trampoline can dispatch the loop off-main
beads.body: workers/cron has never dispatched anything — GITHUB_PAT was never set and every fire is a silent 401. The loop needs it: GitHub runs schedule: only from the default branch, and the loop's state lives on a feature branch. Fine-grained PAT, this repo, Actions:write, nothing else.

beads.title: Which coupling shape? A shared world, a protocol, a compiler, or migrations over live data
beads.body: OPERATOR'S CALL (CLOSED-LOOP.md 11.1). This repo has 5 of the 7 characteristics of scale and is missing exactly the two that produce the feeling — irreducible coupling and an unholdable spec — ON PURPOSE. 60 of 80 surfaces depend on nothing. Reintroducing coupling is a real loss of a property currently enjoyed and should be spent knowingly.

beads.title: May the loop re-publish an existing site nobody asked it to touch?
beads.body:
OPERATOR'S CALL (CLOSED-LOOP.md 11.2). Instinct: yes where the plan was written in the requester's own thread and they saw it; no where an agent invented it unilaterally. That is a judgement about users, not about code.

DROPPED: MOOT, not answered. Greenfield removes the situation: the loop no longer touches sites anyone asked for, so there is no case in which it might re-publish one. Deleting the question beats deciding it. Recorded rather than erased because the reasoning is what makes the deletion legible.

beads.title: A build concluded 'this build cannot reach poly.pizza' and published it as a general claim
beads.body: True of that run. Wrong as a general claim, and nothing in the system could tell it otherwise because nothing in the system remembered. The agent spent several turns writing an OBJ parser and a file-upload button to work around a fetch failure the harness had already hit and not recorded. THIS BEAD IS THE FIX: a dead-end is read before work starts and is never schedulable.

beads.title: GitHub runs schedule: only from the default branch
beads.body: Three ideas-bot workflows carried a schedule: block and not one ever fired. Every post the account made was a side effect of a push trigger. When the branch merged and the pushes stopped, the posts stopped dead 14 hours before anyone asked why — and the merge made the dead schedules LOOK alive on main. Cadence for anything living off main goes through workers/cron.

beads.title: A squash merge is one commit touching every file the branch ever added
beads.body: Not a merge commit — git diff-tree prints nothing for those, which is why real merges skip safely. A squash is one ordinary single-parent commit, so a path-triggered workflow sees all forty-odd files at once and reruns work weeks late at full agent cost. lab-build.yml carries an explicit merge-day guard for exactly this. Any loop workflow triggered by a path needs the same guard.

beads.title: wrangler deploy does not work from the sandbox — no Cloudflare auth
beads.body: Nor do live PDS/Bluesky writes or remote D1 writes. The deploy workflows ARE the network: to deploy, push to a branch the workflow recognises. Do not spend turns debugging credentials that are not there.

beads.title: Green is not proof: a deploy binds the custom domain or it changed nothing
beads.body: If wrangler.jsonc name is not the worker owning the live custom domain, wrangler deploy updates a stray <name>.workers.dev worker: the run goes green and the live site never changes. Verify by confirming the log binds '<domain> (custom domain)'.

beads.title: Attach loop.mino.mobi as a custom domain (dashboard-only)
beads.body: loop.mino.mobi did not resolve on 2026-08-04, probed from the sandbox with sibling hosts on the same zone answering 200. This is a NEW domain, not an adoption. Attaching one is dashboard-only per DEPLOYS.md 7, so the first deploy-loop run may go green having bound nothing. The route is declared in loop/wrangler.jsonc anyway, which is what makes every later deploy re-bind it. When it is attached and a run has bound it, remove the continue-on-error from the verify step in deploy-loop.yml — otherwise a silent unbinding passes forever.

beads.title: Build the real judge probes: loads, interactive, no console errors, frame budget, keyboard, 380px
beads.body: The probe signal today measures liveness of the LOOP (does the graph lint, did the gate pass), not quality of an ARTIFACT. Naming that distinction is the difference between a judge and a smoke test. These are the artifact probes.

beads.title: wrangler DOES create a new custom domain on deploy — DEPLOYS.md 7 overstates the dashboard-only rule
beads.body: Measured 2026-08-04 on loop.mino.mobi, a hostname that did not resolve before the run. wrangler deploy printed 'Deployed loop triggers / loop.mino.mobi (custom domain)' and the domain came up on its own. DEPLOYS.md 7 lists 'attach / detach custom domains' as dashboard-only; that is right for DETACHING and for moving a domain between workers, but a NEW hostname on a zone already in the account is created by the deploy from the routes[] declaration. Two things follow. First: the first deploy's verify step will still fail, because DNS takes ~10s to resolve and Cloudflare then serves error 1104 for a few minutes while the certificate is issued — attempts 1-2 got NXDOMAIN, 3-5 got 500, and the site answered 200 a few minutes later. Do not diagnose that as a binding failure. Second: the honest check is the wrangler log line, not the curl.

beads.title: DECIDED: the loop runs on a standalone greenfield project, not on community submissions
beads.body: Two reasons, and the second is the larger one. (1) The lab factory's sites are strangers' requests — their projects. An unattended wave of turns is a bad fit for work someone else asked for. (2) THE JUDGE. CLOSED-LOOP 3 is the real blocker: nothing in this repo scores whether a thing is good. On a requested website, better can only be scored by a model against a rubric — the least trustworthy instrument available, needing the most calibration, on work we can least afford to get wrong. Choosing our own target lets us choose a domain with an ORACLE: a score that is not a model's opinion. That converts the hardest unbuilt component into a cheap one. THE COST, stated plainly: the 542-concept pool and the 59 BRIEF.md handoffs were the abundant backlog long-horizon work needs. Greenfield starts with an empty ready queue, and the outbox gate structurally forbids an agent filling it. That is why the planner role becomes necessary rather than optional.

beads.title: Choose the greenfield target — this also settles the coupling shape
beads.body: Greenfield collapses the target choice and CLOSED-LOOP 11.1 into ONE decision. Criteria: an oracle (a score that is not a model's opinion); enough depth that turn 30 has real work; the coupling the estate deliberately lacks; self-contained (no third-party rights, no live data, runs in the sandbox); and able to fail visibly, or it is not an experiment. Recommendation offered and NOT taken: an interpreter and a compiler for one small language, cross-checked by differential testing on generated programs. Operator is describing a different target — pressure-test it against the criteria above and say where it is weak BEFORE committing turns.

beads.title: The planner role: a decomposer that turns a spec into an epic tree
beads.body: Does not exist. The fleet half is built (loop-work); the crew half is not. Greenfield has no inherited backlog, so something must produce one. Needs its own workflow (loop-plan.yml), and it must NOT be the same agent that implements.

beads.title: Generalise the promotion gate from 'not its own work' to 'not a bead it authored'
beads.body: Today loop-apply-outbox.mjs creates every agent proposal as 'proposed', full stop. Correct and too strict for unattended greenfield: nothing would ever become ready without a human at the keyboard. The right rule is that no agent may promote a bead IT AUTHORED — checkable from the actor field the ledger already records, and exactly the crew/fleet split (designer != implementer != reviewer). This is a RELAXATION OF A SAFETY PROPERTY: do not ship it before phase 1 has run human-promoted at least once. Earn it.

beads.title: foam-factorio — production inside the lattice, and the loop's target
beads.body: Sources, processors, defenses and sinks summoned into the voronoi foam as Platonic cells. Stays a puzzle platformer, not a sandbox. Chosen over a compiler, a solver family and a research graph because it is the only candidate that is testable (foam already carries a constructive solvability proof), attractive (strangers click a first-person 3D puzzle; nobody visits a compiler), and deep enough that the agents will genuinely struggle.

beads.title: The summon primitive: Platonic cells from a seed constellation
beads.body: A cell's face normals ARE its neighbour directions, so the constellation is the dual solid's vertices. Exact for all five solids at every aniso tested. verify() is the machine half of the judge for this mechanic: a summon either produced the solid it claimed or it did not, and that is a number.

beads.title: Naive seed constellations are 22 degrees wrong — and the CUBE still looks perfect
beads.body: foam's metric is anisotropic (aniso 2.2), so the bisector normal is M*n, NOT n. Placing neighbours at unit directions times a common radius rotates every off-axis face by 22 degrees. A cube survives because axis-aligned normals are the only ones M cannot rotate — which is the worst outcome, since the cube is what anyone tries first. The wrong conclusion this invites is 'voronoi cells just aren't regular'. They are. n = 2r*Minv*u / (u^T*Minv*u). Do not re-derive this; do not trust a cube as evidence.

beads.title: Math.acos(dot) reports 1.2e-6 degrees of noise for exact unit vectors
beads.body: acos is ill-conditioned near 1: for vectors agreeing to machine precision, dot = 1-eps with eps~2e-16 and acos returns sqrt(2*eps) ~ 2e-8 rad ~ 1.2e-6 degrees. That reads as a real error and invites either 'fixing' exact geometry or widening the tolerance until the check stops catching the 22-degree bug it exists for. Use atan2(|cross|, |dot|) — accurate all the way to zero.

beads.title: A verifier grading against the wrong reference failed correct geometry by exactly the yaw angle
beads.body: constellation() did not return its own rotate parameter, so verify() compared a yawed solid against unrotated normals and reported 36 degrees of error for a 36 degree yaw. A checker that FAILS CORRECT WORK is worse than no checker: it retires a mechanic that was fine, and the retirement looks like evidence.

beads.title: A loop commit under foam/** deploys nothing — deploy-foam is branch-locked
beads.body: deploy-foam.yml triggers only on claude/voronoi-foam-interactive-keo0uy. The loop runs on its own branch, so adding foam/** to the loop's writes wakes NO new workflow — verified with the blast-radius checker. This is the right shape: a human merge is the publication step, so a human decides what strangers see. It is also a hard constraint on feedback latency, and it is why the audience ladder cannot be a per-turn gate.

beads.title: Atomic multi-insert: reformPocket for a whole constellation, all-or-nothing
beads.body: reformPocket(pocket, point) inserts ONE seed and re-derives closure + nav. A half-inserted dodecahedron is not a dodecahedron, so a constellation must land as one transaction with a single closure-and-nav gate at the end — not 13 sequential calls, each of which can refuse. Refusal must roll the whole thing back and say which seed collided.

beads.title: Summon legality as a decidable predicate in a real pocket
beads.body: clearanceNeeded() gives the radius that must be free, but the real test is against a pocket's existing seeds AND the indestructible hull. Make 'can I build here?' answerable BEFORE attempting, so the UI can show buildable space rather than failing on click. Needing clear ground to place a factory is the oldest rule in the genre — the constraint is the mechanic.

beads.title: Object kinds: sources, processors, defenses, sinks as cell roles
beads.body: Which solid means what, what a recipe looks like, and how a role is marked in the render (baseSeedCount already amber-shifts planted chambers — the existing hook). Defenses are the one that may imply an adversary, which would turn the build certificate into a strategy rather than a plan. That is a much larger commitment than the other three — see FACTORIO.md 7.2.

beads.title: Production feasibility oracle — the algebra
beads.body: Sources emit rates, processors transform, sinks demand: a factory is a flow network and satisfiability is a feasibility question over a small non-negative linear system. Exact, cheap, no search, no heuristics. The MARGIN by which a recipe set is satisfiable is also a difficulty dial, the way parMin/parTarget band the walk today.

beads.title: THE BUILD CERTIFICATE — a legal ordering over a self-modifying lattice
beads.body: Prove there exists an ordered sequence of walks and summons such that each summon is legal when attempted, the walker can reach each site GIVEN THE LATTICE AS IT STANDS, and the finished production graph meets demand. The difficulty is that the actions mutate the state space they are searched over: summoning reforms the lattice, so placing an object can open a route, close one, or strand the walker. This is a planning problem over a self-modifying graph — a real CS problem, not a content problem. This is where the turns go.

beads.title: Generation searches build PLANS, not just salts
beads.body: generatePocket retries maxSalt=24 seeds until a walk certificate exists. The factorio generator must retry until a PLAN exists, and that search is orders of magnitude larger. Keep the invariant that no unproven pocket is ever returned.

beads.title: Par and the difficulty band generalise to build cost
beads.body: Par counts breaches today. It becomes a cost over breaches + summons + distance, and the puzzle band moves with it. Without this there is no difficulty oracle for factory levels and 'par in band' stops meaning anything.

beads.title: Per-turn frame-budget number under N summons on mobile
beads.body: A dodecahedron is 13 seeds; ten is +130 against a base pocket of ~294, and buildComplex runs on every summon while mobile performance is a hard requirement. Rich factories and the frame budget pull against each other. Turn this from a discipline into a NUMBER the judge reads, or gate 7 does not exist.

beads.title: PHASE 0 — will strangers actually vote? Ship the pairwise page against hand-made variants
beads.body: The ladder needs N. If foam draws five visitors a week it never resolves and the programme stalls on a distribution problem wearing an engineering costume. Ship the A/B comparison against two HAND-MADE variants and count votes. Randomise order, record it, and check the control: if position predicts preference better than version does, the signal is noise. A negative result here ends the programme for zero model spend — which is the best kind of phase, and the reason this is P0.

beads.title: How do strangers vote, and where is it stored?
beads.body: OPERATOR'S CALL. atpolls-db exists with 8 dependents and poll/ already does anonymous voting properly. Reusing it buys infrastructure and buys blast radius. Deliberate coupling is wanted (CLOSED-LOOP 11.1); accidental coupling is not.

beads.title: Replace the judge's 'rubric' signal with human pairwise preference?
beads.body: OPERATOR'S CALL, and there is a KNOWN INCONSISTENCY until it is made: FACTORIO.md 5 argues the quality signal should be pairwise preference between consecutive turns' output, while .github/loop/config.json still lists signals [probes, rubric, adversarial]. The config was left alone deliberately rather than edited to match the prose — it is the live control surface and this is a design decision, not a typo. The argument for the swap: the programme's question is 'does turn 20 beat turn 19', and a pairwise A/B asks exactly that, with no rubric to write and no calibration to do. The argument against: pairwise needs traffic (see the phase 0 bead) and settles over days rather than per turn, so it cannot be a per-turn gate. Resolve this before enabling the loop, or the config and the design record disagree in public.

beads.title: AUDIT: the ready queue held zero class-A requirements — it looked healthy and was starved
beads.body: Applied the Definition of Ready to the eight beads sitting in the queue an hour after authoring them. Two were PHASES pretending to be tickets (fail R1 one-turn and R2 names-its-gate). Three were class B — they BUILD gates, so they define what done means and an agent must not self-serve them. Two were human-only infrastructure with no machine gate. One was already finished and nobody had closed it. Net class-A count available to an unattended fleet: ZERO. The queue length said eight. This is the exact failure the WBS names: starved and idle look identical from outside, and a rich backlog with no schedulable work is a stalled programme reading as a healthy one. Count class A, not beads.

beads.title: The promotion rule is the loop's GAIN control — it is why nothing has run away yet
beads.body: The chain grows by BRANCHING FACTOR, not by speed. Gain = expected successor turns per turn: below 1 it dies out, at 1 it is self-sustaining forever, above 1 it is exponential. Today gain is structurally ZERO for anything the fleet produces, because loop-apply-outbox.mjs creates every agent proposal as 'proposed' and never 'ready' — the loop drains what a human put in the queue and halts. That rule was written as a quality gate; it turns out to be the strongest regulator in the system. WBS phase 3.2, relaxing it to 'not a bead it authored', is EXACTLY the change that lifts gain off zero. It must not ship unless something else holds gain below one.

beads.title: A rate limit is a saturation, not a regulator — and running at it destroys the measurement
beads.body: Using the account's usage limit as the governor fails twice. Informationally: pinned at the ceiling, utilisation reads 100% whether the loop is producing or spinning, so throughput becomes a property of the limit rather than of the work — and this programme exists to measure whether the work keeps paying. Practically: the limit is shared with the operator, so a regulator whose set-point is 'all of it' collides rather than regulates. The honest version is a HEADROOM RESERVE: target a fraction, observe consumption, back off when the operator is active.

beads.title: Adopt the three-mechanism regulator: enabled / SEATS / lease?
beads.body: OPERATOR'S CALL. Three mechanisms, three questions: may it run at all (enabled, built); how hard (SEATS — a licence to occupy one concurrent turn, typed by role, allocated against demand); until when (a lease with an expiry the reactor refuses to dispatch past). Seats replace the spend-bucket proposal: a bucket regulates a rate, but seats regulate a POPULATION, which is the thing that actually needs bounding (lp-CORRECTION) and is one legible integer. A short lease with many seats is a redline sprint; a long lease with few seats is a sustained run — same two knobs, opposite settings, and neither requires guessing a turn count. Adopting this deprecates turnsPerDay and maxConcurrentWork in favour of a typed seat pool.

beads.title: Per-turn spend accounting: make cost an observable, not an assumption
beads.body: claude -p --max-budget-usd bounds one turn; nothing accumulates it. Without accumulation there is no bucket, no headroom reserve and no honest cost curve — and CLOSED-LOOP 10's estimate stays the weakest number in the programme. The turn record in runs.jsonl already has a slot for it.

beads.title: The clock half of the hybrid: cron-driven refill so the chain cannot self-sustain
beads.body: The chain is built; the clock is not. Hybrid: the chain may continue while tokens remain, and when the bucket empties it stops and waits for the clock to refill. Burst latency when there is budget, externally-bounded rate when there is not. Depends on CRON_GITHUB_PAT, which has never been set — workers/cron has dispatched nothing in its entire life.

beads.title: CORRECTION: bound the POPULATION, not the gain — branching is the point
beads.body: Supersedes lp-1dfea1's conclusion, not its analysis. That bead was right that the promotion rule sets the loop's gain, and WRONG that gain is what to bound — it conflated backlog growth with runaway spend, and those are separable. Gain above one grows the READY QUEUE, which costs bytes of JSONL and is an ASSET: long-horizon agent work is starved by too little backlog, not endangered by too much. What must be capped is WORK IN FLIGHT. Bound the worker population and the branching factor can be whatever the work demands, because throughput is set by headcount rather than backlog depth. That is how every organisation with a ticket tracker already works: nobody panics at ten thousand open tickets, they staff to a number. Seats, not gain.

beads.title: Typed seat pools and the org chart: plan / implement / review / judge
beads.body: Fungible seats fail specifically: all-available plus demand reading 'implement' means the planner never runs and the queue starves; the other way, the backlog inflates and nothing gets built. THE RATIO BETWEEN plan AND implement SEATS IS THE PRODUCER/CONSUMER RATIO — too many of one blocks on the other, expressed as headcount rather than as hope. Seat class and model tier must be separable so implement can be Opus while judge and routine verification are not.

beads.title: The allocator: seats assigned per tick against observed demand, with backpressure
beads.body: This is where 'demand-driven' lives. Shallow queue -> plan seats. Deep queue -> implement seats. Proposals piling up unpromoted -> review seats. Turns completing unscored -> judge seats. Repeated gate failures -> NOTHING: that is a stop condition, not a staffing problem, and an allocator that responds to failure by staffing harder spends fastest exactly when it is working worst. Backpressure is what makes an unbounded queue safe: a deep queue WITHDRAWS plan seats, so the planner cannot inflate a backlog nobody consumes.

beads.title: Promotion priced at a review seat, not prohibited
beads.body: Replaces the total prohibition with a price. review seats are deliberately scarcer than implement seats, so the rate at which the loop can feed itself is a dial rather than a cliff. The narrow invariant that must survive: NO AGENT REVIEWS A BEAD IT AUTHORED. Class B stays never-agent-promotable — an agent that can author the gate judging it has no gate, and no seat price fixes that.

beads.title: Throttled is a STATE, not a failure — release seats, hold the queue, resume
beads.body: Today a 429 mid-turn would surface as a failed turn, and a run of them would trip repeatedGateFailures: the loop concluding it is broken when it is merely throttled, stopping for the wrong reason and leaving a misleading record. Degradation ladder in preference order: fewer seats; cheaper seats for mechanical work (gates, lint, regeneration, probes do not need the strongest model); wait for the window (the queue is durable, nothing is lost); meter to the API as an explicit spend decision. CLOSED-LOOP 8 declines exactly one option — multiple subscription accounts — and that stays declined. Nothing else here is evasion.

beads.title: The seat board: make loop.mino.mobi show motion, not a snapshot
beads.body: The seat model is also what makes the run worth watching. Show the seats and who holds them, what each is working on, what closed in the last hour, what was spawned behind it, and how the allocator is currently split. A bead retiring and three appearing behind it is the programme's heartbeat and it is currently invisible — the page renders a graph, not motion. This is the difference between a dashboard and something you leave open.

beads.title: BUG IN THE BUILD: loop-work commits the ledger and graph.json — guaranteed conflict at N>1
beads.body: loop-work.yml applies its own outbox to beads.jsonl AND regenerates loop/data/graph.json AND commits both. At one seat that is fine and it is what shipped. At six seats it is a guaranteed conflict on EVERY turn, on the two files every turn touches — and the graph.json conflict is meaningless, since the file is a pure function of the ledger. Turns commit SOURCES; the integrator regenerates derived files once, after the merge. This will be the first thing that breaks when seats go above one.

beads.title: Conflicts are re-work, not resolution — and that is only affordable because of the DoR
beads.body: A turn that lands conflicting is DISCARDED and its bead returns to ready. No hand resolution, ever. This is affordable precisely because R1 says a requirement is one turn and R6 says a failed attempt leaves the tree as it found it — re-running 20 minutes of agent work is cheaper than a human resolving a semantic conflict, and hand resolution is the expensive resource being conserved. Corollary: repeated conflicts between the same two requirements mean R4 was WRONG about them being independent. Conflict frequency is a quality metric for the requirement factory, not just a cost.

beads.title: A human cannot perceive one turn's improvement — the SPRINT is the judge unit
beads.body: The audience ladder asks which of two versions is better. Turn N against turn N-1 is far below the resolution of that judgement: strangers would be voting on noise and the ladder would measure nothing. A sprint is a coherent increment — several turns integrated, gated, deployed — and that is perceptible. So sprint = merge epoch = deploy unit = judge unit, one concept doing four jobs, and the curve becomes quality against SPRINT rather than turn. Turn count stays an observable: how much was spent to move one sprint is exactly the cost-per-improvement figure the programme wants.

beads.title: Confirm the third surface: plant.minomobi.com, seeded from foam
beads.body: OPERATOR'S CALL, and it corrects an obvious-but-wrong instinct. plant.mino.mobi would put agent-generated content inside the SSO cookie's Domain=.mino.mobi scope, inside the auth worker's wildcard origin allowlist, and inside the operator's reputation — the three reasons LAB-FACTORY 3 gives for why agent-written pages must not live there. And minomobi.com/plant/ is served by the lab worker, so a loop push would fire deploy-lab and republish forty tenant sites every sprint. A separate worker on plant.minomobi.com gives the quarantine without the blast radius (labglass/os-api precedent). Name: foam's third shiva tool is PLANT, and a plant is a factory.

beads.title: Path leases: the allocator refuses to co-schedule intersecting path sets
beads.body: R3 (bounded paths) and R4 (independent) already carry the mechanism as an aspiration. Enforce it and conflicts are not resolved, not merged and not detected — they are NOT CREATED. Same insight the lab factory runs on (disjoint tenant dirs never conflict), applied at finer grain because this work is not naturally disjoint. Does not cover semantic breakage; removes the bulk cheaply using a field requirements must carry anyway.

beads.title: The integrator: one merge seat, one run per sprint, deadline-bounded
beads.body: Collect branches; ABANDON turns still running at the deadline rather than waiting (one slow turn must not hold six — this is the step that will be got wrong first); merge conflict-free first then by priority then reject; apply all outboxes in bead-id order as ONE ledger write; regenerate derived artifacts once; preflight + blast-radius; push to the plant branch; record the sprint for the judge. Cost: one integrator run per SPRINT, not per turn — at six seats that is 17% overhead instead of 100%.

beads.title: Sprint identity: sprint id on every work order, branch name and run record
beads.body: There is no sprint concept anywhere in the current build. Everything downstream — the barrier, the integrator, sprint-scoped judging, the curve's x-axis — needs turns to know which sprint they belong to and to branch from that sprint's base rather than from moving trunk.

beads.title: gitattributes: *.jsonl merge=union as the net under the ledger
beads.body: Git's built-in union driver takes lines from both sides, which is the correct resolution for an append-only log. Only safe when the two sides append DIFFERENT records — two turns patching the same bead would have their order decided arbitrarily. Path leasing plus one-bead-per-seat is what makes that not arise. The union driver is the net, not the plan.

beads.title: Publish the loop's own architecture: the machine diagram and the org chart
beads.body: The page showed the loop's STATE and nothing about its STRUCTURE. Adds three panels rendered from config rather than hardcoded, so the page cannot drift from the governor it describes: a control diagram (operator inputs above the line, reactor, allocator, seats, graph, barrier, and the two feedback edges that make it a loop rather than a pipeline); the org chart as cards; and a 'how the gain is controlled' panel separating the three things routinely confused for one — the queue may grow freely, work in flight may not, and feeding itself is priced rather than forbidden. Seats are marked PROPOSED because nothing is wired to them yet. The refusal edge is drawn as a crossed-out line: gate failures never buy staff.

beads.title: loop.mino.mobi /health and /api can lag the ledger by up to 5 minutes, by design
beads.body: Checked immediately after a deploy, /health reported 62 beads while the committed graph.json said 63, and one edge node served an /api/graph.json with no seats field while others served it correctly. Not a bug: worker.js sets cache-control 'max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300' on those routes, which explicitly permits serving a stale copy for five further minutes while revalidating, and Cloudflare edge nodes propagate independently. Two consequences. (1) A probe run right after a deploy can report a stale count that looks exactly like a data bug — add a cache-buster query before concluding anything. (2) DO NOT build an automated gate that compares the live endpoint against the repo: it would flake for five minutes after every single sprint. Compare against the committed artifact instead — that is what gen-loop-data --check already does.

beads.title: THE BUDGET METER IS IN THE WRONG PLACE — turns are counted from runs.jsonl, which only the JUDGE writes
beads.body: Found by rehearsing the chain end to end, not by reading it. loop-tick computes turns = runs.length and today = runs filtered by timestamp, and runs.jsonl is appended ONLY by loop-judge. So if the judge does not run — trigger does not fire, enabled check trips, push does not wake it, job fails — the reactor keeps reporting '0 turns so far' and dispatching FOREVER. hardStopTurns and turnsPerDay both become inert, silently, while spend continues. This is the repo's recurring failure wearing new clothes: green, healthy, and metering nothing (see workers/cron). THE METER MUST BE AT THE POINT OF SPEND: tick should append to its own turns ledger when it ISSUES a work order, not learn the count later from a downstream component that may never run. Quality measurement and budget accounting must not share a writer.

beads.title: The reactor is blind to requirement class — its first-ever pick was a class-B bead
beads.body: Rehearsed with enabled flipped in the working tree: the very first bead loop-tick chose to dispatch was lp-f25c2f 'Atomic multi-insert', tagged class-b. LOOP-WBS 2.3 says class B builds a GATE — it defines what done means — and must never be fleet-dispatched, because an agent that can redefine done has no gate. The taxonomy exists in a document and in bead TAGS; the scheduler reads neither. So the loop's first autonomous act would have been the one act the design forbids. readyQueue must filter on class, and a bead with no class tag must be treated as unschedulable rather than as class A — fail closed, the same rule the blast-radius checker uses.

beads.title: The chain itself works: tick to work order to outbox to ledger to next tick
beads.body: Rehearsed locally with a simulated agent outbox. The reactor dispatched and wrote a work order; the outbox validated and applied; three records appended; the work order and outbox were both consumed so the concurrency slot was released; the target closed with evidence and its run number; THE GATE HELD — the agent's proposal landed as 'proposed' and its finding as 'done'; and the next tick picked up the next bead. The plumbing is sound. What is not sound is what it chose to do and how it counts — see the two dead-ends filed alongside this.

beads.title: actions/checkout's persisted credentials override a remote URL's — the PAT was present and never used
beads.body: The loop's first live dispatch passed all four gates, committed the work order, and then died on four 403s: 'Permission to minormobius/agent01.git denied to github-actions[bot]'. The diagnosis is NOT a missing secret — OS_AGENT_GITHUB_TOKEN was set and the workflow's own -z guard passed. actions/checkout stores its token as an http.<host>.extraheader in the LOCAL git config, and that header takes precedence over credentials embedded in a remote URL. So 'git remote set-url origin https://x-access-token:PAT@github.com/...' was silently ignored and the push authenticated as the default Actions bot, which cannot push. Fix: persist-credentials: false on the checkout in every loop workflow. THE MISLEADING PART is that the error names the bot, which reads as 'the wrong token was configured' when in fact the right token was configured and overridden. Anything in this repo that pushes from Actions with a PAT needs this.

Since a turn with only Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep cannot run `node`/`cmp`, and this turn discovered a prior 'done' bead's evidence files simply did not exist, the judge (which presumably has broader tooling) should at minimum stat() each evidence path before accepting a done outcome, independent of running the full gate command. beads.title: a vague idea with no gate
A scripted edit put NUL bytes into a .mjs source and every test still passed
beads.body: Three NUL bytes replaced the SPACES in mintId's seed template: `${bead.title}\0${bead.created}\0${bead.actor}`. Node parsed it fine (they sit inside a template literal, so they are just characters), all 44 selftests passed, lint was clean, and the loop ran. THE ONLY SIGNAL WAS git reporting 'Bin 16405 -> 18017 bytes' on a JavaScript file in a commit stat. Two lessons. (1) Passing tests do not prove a source file is well-formed — they prove it PARSES and BEHAVES, which is a weaker claim than it feels like. (2) Read the diffstat: 'Bin' on a text file is git telling you something is wrong in the only place it can. Also note what it silently changed: the id derivation moved from space-joined to NUL-joined, so ids minted before and after differ for identical inputs. Harmless here because ids are stored rather than recomputed, but a content-derived identifier whose derivation drifts is a nasty class of bug.

beads.title: Every HALT went red — the step re-ran the script to explain itself, and the explanation exited 3 too
beads.body: loop-tick exits 3 on halt DELIBERATELY: a halt is a correct outcome, and a red run every time a stop condition works is how a team learns to ignore red runs. The Decide step wrapped that in set +e / CODE=$? / set -e, then — inside the halt branch, with errexit restored — ran 'loop-tick.mjs --json' a SECOND time to read the reason. That call also exits 3. So the step died at the exact moment it was explaining why it had stopped, the run went red, GITHUB_OUTPUT was never written, and the downstream 'if acted == plan' never fired. The plan request had already been written to disk and was simply never committed. Fix: one invocation, '--write --json > file', branch on the captured code. LESSON: a script with a meaningful non-zero exit needs its CALLER audited too — the design was right and the shell around it silently inverted it for two turns.

beads.title: clearanceNeeded's Euclidean radius is sound-but-loose against the real anisotropic gap, not a bug

Checked whether that's a bug: since aniso=2.2>1, anisotropic distance >= Euclidean distance for every displacement, so 'no pre-existing seed within Euclidean radius extent+1.5' always implies 'no pre-existing seed within anisotropic distance 1.5' — the bound is conservative-but-valid, never unsafe. It can be loose (reject some builds a tighter ellipsoidal check would allow) because a single scalar radius cannot be tight against an anisotropic exclusion zone without clearanceNeeded returning a direction-dependent shape, which is a bigger API change than this scope. Not proposed as a fix; scoped instead as a soundness property worth pinning (see the selfCompatible/pairGap proposal).

That is the same formula reformPocket uses for real (foam/foamworld.js:721-722) but it lives nowhere reusable — solids.mjs exports clearanceNeeded() (a Euclidean radius, see the decision above) but nothing that runs the actual anisotropic check. beads.title: Export the real anisotropic seed-gap check from solids.mjs: seedGap, selfCompatible, pairGap
beads.body:
Bounded paths: plant/solids.mjs, plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs only. Add three exports to plant/solids.mjs: `seedGap(a, b, aniso)` — the exact anisotropic distance between two points, matching reformPocket's real check byte-for-byte (foam/foamworld.js:721-722: scale the y-difference by Math.sqrt(aniso), then Math.hypot) — do not reimplement the formula differently, replicate it; `selfCompatible(con, minSeedGap = 1.5)` — true iff every pair of con.seeds (centre + all neighbours) has seedGap >= minSeedGap; `pairGap(conA, conB)` — the minimum seedGap over every (a in conA.seeds, b in conB.seeds) pair, for checking two adjacent summons don't collide with EACH OTHER (constellation()'s own clearanceNeeded only covers one solid against pre-existing single seeds, never two five-plus-seed constellations against each other). Then: (1) replace the two inline anisotropic-gap loops already in the selftest's clearance section (~lines 97-121, for tetrahedron r=1.0 and icosahedron r=0.35) with calls to selfCompatible, keeping the same pass/fail expectations; (2) extend that section to also assert selfCompatible for cube and octahedron (pick radii that bracket true/false the way the existing two cases do, e.g. by scaling from the tetrahedron/icosahedron radii already proven to work); (3) add a pairGap case with two fixed, deterministic centres (no Math.random) — one far enough apart to be compatible, one close enough to collide. Ties to the DEAD-END that naive constellations are 22 degrees wrong (docs/../foam/FACTORIO.md §1, restated in plant/CLAUDE.md) and to the AUDIT finding that a starved ready queue looked healthy — this closes an actual gap between what plant/CLAUDE.md documents reformPocket doing and what solids.mjs lets a caller check before ever touching a real pocket. Reversible: pure additive exports plus additive/replaced test assertions; a failed attempt is a git-revertable diff to two files.

[turn 3 — done] Added seedGap(a,b,aniso), selfCompatible(con,minSeedGap=1.5) and pairGap(conA,conB) to plant/solids.mjs. seedGap replicates reformPocket's own refusal check (foam/foamworld.js:721-722) structurally byte-for-byte: scale the y-difference by Math.sqrt(aniso), then combine via Math.hypot (reformPocket compares the squared form against 2.25; seedGap returns the un-squared distance so callers compare directly against 1.5). selfCompatible checks every pair of con.seeds (centre + all neighbours, not just neighbour-neighbour pairs like the old inline test did); pairGap takes the minimum seedGap over the full cross-product of two constellations' seeds, using conA.aniso. In plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs: replaced both inline anisotropic-gap loops (tetrahedron r=1.0, icosahedron r=0.35) with selfCompatible calls, keeping identical pass/fail expectations; added a direct seedGap-vs-independently-written-formula check; added a cube r=1.0 (self-compatible) and octahedron r=0.3 (self-collides) pair to broaden solid coverage beyond tetrahedron/icosahedron; added two pairGap cases with fixed deterministic centres (two tetrahedra 20 apart -> compatible, two tetrahedra 0.5 apart -> collide). I do not have Bash in this turn and could not execute 'node plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs' myself, so the GATE is unverified in-turn -- this is the same structural limitation filed previously for lp-dfad42. I hand-derived the expected numbers before choosing radii so the new assertions have real margin, not a coin-flip: cube r=1.0 gives an EXACT minimum own-seed gap of 2*r=2.0 (centre to an x- or z-axis neighbour, the two axes aniso never touches -- no approximation involved, this one is algebraically exact), well clear of the 1.5 threshold; octahedron r=0.3 gives an approximate minimum own-seed gap of ~1.90*r=0.57 (derived analytically from the constellation() formula for the octahedron's 8 equal-magnitude-component normals), safely under 1.5 with a >2x margin so small arithmetic slips can't flip the verdict. The pairGap far case (centres 20 apart) is bounded rigorously via triangle inequality using each tetrahedron's own Euclidean extent (~2.1), leaving >15 units of margin; the close case (centres 0.5 apart) is guaranteed to collide because the two constellations' CENTRES alone are only 0.5 apart, which is already one of the pairs pairGap minimizes over, independent of any neighbour-position arithmetic. All of this is reasoned from the same closed-form algebra solids.mjs already documents (M-inverse bisector formula), not run.

beads.body:
Bounded paths: plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs only, no changes to plant/solids.mjs. The 'determinism and orientation' block (~lines 75-88) checks that a yawed constellation stays exact (verify(r1).ok) using only 'cube'. plant/solids.mjs's own header comment names the exact trap this repeats: cube's normals are axis-aligned, the one case an anisotropic metric cannot rotate wrong — 'the worst possible outcome... the first solid anyone tries is the cube, it looks perfect, and the bug waits in the second one.' beads.title: class-A's gate certifies no regression, not the new behaviour — the agent writes the assertions it is graded by
beads.body:
Observed at the moment of promoting lp-6b641c/lp-687d8d/lp-138b76, the loop's first self-made queue.

All three name the SAME gate: 'node plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs'. It exists today and it passes today, which is what makes them class-A. But their bounded paths include plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs itself, so the agent adds the assertions and then is graded by them. The gate proves NOTHING NEW BROKE; it does not prove the new exports are correct, because nothing tested them until the same turn wrote both sides.

This is not a reason to refuse them — a gate that catches regression is worth running, and refusing every ticket whose test does not pre-exist means only work with a pre-written test is ever schedulable, which is a much smaller loop than the one being built. It IS the reason to keep the judge's adversarial signal, and it is the sharpest argument for a REVIEW seat that reads the diff rather than trusting the exit code.

Ranked by exposure: lp-6b641c is worst (new executable exports, self-authored tests). lp-687d8d and lp-138b76 only widen coverage of code that already exists and is already verified against a closed-form answer, so their self-certification is much weaker tea.

Watch for: a turn that makes the gate pass by weakening an assertion rather than by doing the work. That is the specific cheat this shape permits and the one the verdict should look for.

[turn ? — done] Operator dry-run of the ask channel, applied through the real validator rather than hand-written into the ledger — the same code path an agent's outbox takes.

beads.title: pairGap uses conA.aniso, not an aniso argument of its own
beads.body: The ticket's signature is pairGap(conA, conB) -- two args, no aniso. Two constellations being checked against each other are expected to live in the same pocket and therefore share one metric, so I read it off conA rather than requiring the caller to pass it again or silently defaulting to something that could disagree with either constellation's own aniso. Rejected: a third optional aniso parameter (drifts from the ticket's stated signature for no real benefit) and asserting conA.aniso === conB.aniso (extra failure mode for a case that in practice can't arise -- both constellations come from the same constellation() call site in the same pocket). This reverses easily if a caller ever legitimately mixes metrics: add the parameter back with conA.aniso as its default.

beads.title: cube's minimum self-seed-gap is EXACTLY 2*r, no approximation -- because aniso only touches y and cube neighbours never mix y with x or z
beads.body: constellation('cube', {r}) places neighbours at exactly (+-2r,0,0),(0,+-2r,0),(0,0,+-2r) -- the t=2r/q algebra collapses to that because q=1 for an axis-aligned unit normal. The centre-to-x-or-z-neighbour seedGap is then hypot(2r,0,0)=2r with zero anisotropic scaling involved (dy=0), and every other pair (neighbour-neighbour, or centre to a y-axis neighbour) is provably larger since sqrt(aniso)>1 only inflates gaps that involve a y-difference. So for the cube specifically, 'is it self-compatible at minSeedGap m' reduces to the exact closed form r >= m/2 -- no floating-point approximation risk, unlike every other solid in SOLIDS. Worth knowing if a future ticket wants a cheap, exact clearance check for the one solid the anisotropic trap doesn't touch.

beads.title: Add a closed-form fast path or documented formula for cube self-compatibility (r >= minSeedGap/2) alongside the general selfCompatible
beads.body: Filed as a finding on this same turn: cube's own-seed minimum gap is exactly 2*r for any aniso, because its normals are axis-aligned and aniso only scales the y-axis. That's a decidable predicate in closed form, unlike the other four solids. Not urgent -- selfCompatible(con) already gets the right answer for cube today by brute force over 7 seeds, this would only matter if a hot path needed to test many candidate cube radii without allocating a constellation each time.

beads.title: Grant Bash (or a downstream verification turn) to class-A tickets whose GATE is a shell command, or make the gate's in-turn-unverified status explicit in the bead
beads.body: Second turn in a row (after lp-dfad42) where the ticket's own acceptance test (node plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs) could not be run by the turn responsible for satisfying it, because the tool grant is Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep only. This isn't a complaint about this specific ticket -- the port and this export both had enough closed-form structure to hand-verify with real confidence -- but a ticket whose new code is more novel or less analytically tractable than this one would have no way to self-check at all. Either the executing turn for a node-gated class-A bead should get Bash, or the bead should say up front that gate verification happens downstream (CI or the judge) so the turn doesn't have to pretend confidence it can't back up.

beads.title: This turn's own gate is unverifiable in-turn — same shape as lp-dfad42
beads.body: lp-138b76's GATE is 'node plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs' but this turn's tool grant was Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep only, no Bash. The added assertions are a mechanical copy of the existing, already-passing cube yaw block with 'cube'->'icosahedron' and r 1.5->1.2, calling the same constellation()/verify() functions already proven correct for icosahedron elsewhere in the same file (just without rotate) — so confidence is high, but it is inference from adjacent evidence, not execution. Confirms the earlier finding that class-A tickets whose gate is a shell command need either a Bash-equipped turn or an explicit downstream (CI/judge) verification step, not an in-turn assumption that the gate ran.

beads.title: Turn 3's self-authored tests killed 2 of 3 mutants — the survivor is the one behaviour it strengthened
beads.body:
Mutation-tested turn 3's output (lp-6b641c) rather than trusting its green gate, because lp-20c414 flagged that the agent writes the assertions it is graded by.

  seedGap drops the sqrt(aniso) scaling  -> KILLED
  pairGap returns max instead of min     -> KILLED
  selfCompatible skips the centre seed   -> SURVIVED

The survivor matters more than the two kills. selfCompatible's docstring claims it checks 'its centre AND every neighbour', and that IS a deliberate strengthening over the inline loop it replaced, which only checked neighbour-vs-neighbour. The agent widened the contract, documented the widening, and then tested only the part that was already true. Every solid it asserts on has its centre comfortably clear of its own neighbours at r=1.0, so removing the centre from the loop changes no verdict in the suite.

The verdict on the turn is still GOOD: correct against foamworld.js:721-722 (which compares the squared form to 2.25, so the un-squared < 1.5 is exactly equivalent), foam/ untouched, every new positive paired with a CONTROL negative, and the replaced assertions strictly stronger than the ones removed.

The generalisable lesson, which is worth more than the fix: a self-certifying turn tests what it BUILT and under-tests what it CLAIMED. The gap is not in the code, it is between the docstring and the assertions. A review seat should diff those two against each other.

beads.title: Assert selfCompatible's centre-inclusion — the one claim turn 3 documented but did not test
beads.body:
Bounded paths: plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs ONLY. Do not change plant/solids.mjs — the implementation is correct; the suite just cannot tell.

Mutation testing (see lp-c46a0c) showed that changing selfCompatible's loop from con.seeds to con.neighbours — i.e. silently dropping the centre seed it promises to check — leaves every assertion in the suite passing. Its docstring says 'its centre AND every neighbour'; nothing proves the first half.

Add a case where the CENTRE is the violating seed while all neighbour-vs-neighbour gaps stay legal, so selfCompatible must return false for a reason only centre-inclusion can see. A flattened constellation is the natural shape: keep r large enough that the neighbours stay mutually clear, and pick a solid/aniso where at least one neighbour falls within 1.5 of the centre under the anisotropic metric. Assert false, and pair it with a CONTROL that is identical except comfortably clear, asserting true — the file's house style, and the thing that proves the new case fails for the intended reason rather than by accident.

Verify your case actually has teeth before reporting done: it must FAIL if selfCompatible iterates con.neighbours instead of con.seeds. If you cannot construct such a case for any solid, that is a real finding about the geometry — file it as one and say why, rather than forcing a weaker assertion.

beads.title: The reactor was the one writer that pushed without rebasing — a concurrent commit stops the whole chain
beads.body:
Turn 4's verdict woke the tick, the tick correctly decided "dispatch" for turn 5, and then died in its push loop because an operator commit had landed while it was deciding. The chain stopped with a red run on a CORRECT decision.

loop-work and loop-judge both retry as "git pull --rebase && git push". loop-tick retried a bare "git push" four times. Nothing between those attempts can turn a non-fast-forward into a fast-forward, so the retry loop was four guaranteed failures with exponential backoff between them — a backoff that could only ever make the loss slower.

Three things this says beyond the one-line fix:

1. THE RETRY WAS DECORATIVE. It looked like resilience and had none. Backoff without a merge step is a spin. Any retry loop in this repo should be read with the question "what changes between attempts?" — if the answer is nothing, it is not a retry, it is a delay before the same failure.

2. THIS IS THE DESIGNED CASE, ARRIVING EARLY. LOOP-SPRINTS.md plans for six parallel agents on one branch. It took exactly TWO concurrent writers — one human, one reactor — to break it. The path-lease and sprint-barrier machinery is aimed at agents conflicting with each other; nothing is aimed at an operator committing while the loop runs, which is the most ordinary thing that can happen.

3. THE GENERATED FILE CONFLICTS EVERY TIME, and that is fine. loop/data/graph.json is derived from the ledger, so two writers regenerate it from different states and collide on content. It resolves by REGENERATING, never by merging: take either side, run gen-loop-data.mjs --write, continue. That is LOOP-SPRINTS.md's "redo, not resolve" rule meeting its first real conflict, and the rule held.

Recorded separately because it bit while writing this bead: beads.mjs takes its body on the command line, so a body containing backticks is executed by the shell before the CLI ever sees it. This finding's first draft ran "git pull --rebase && git push" as a side effect of being written down. No damage — the pull refused on unstaged changes — but a knowledge tool whose input is shell is a knowledge tool that can act. A --body-file flag would end the whole class.

beads.title: Used r=1.4 for all four newly-swept solids, matching dodecahedron's existing value
beads.body: The ticket allowed 'r=1.4 or whatever keeps the block's existing style'. Kept 1.4 uniformly across all five solids in this block rather than varying r per solid, since the block's purpose is isolating the aniso variable — varying r per solid would conflate two things being tested and wasn't justified by anything in the ticket or the file's existing conventions. Would reverse this only if a future finding shows some solid's constellation() misbehaves specifically at r=1.4 (e.g. a degenerate clearance), which nothing here suggests.

beads.title: Turn 5 completed a coverage matrix with zero marginal detection value — the planner reasoned about the test's shape, not the code's
beads.body:
Turn 5 delivered exactly what lp-687d8d asked: the aniso sweep [1.2, 2.2, 3.5, 8] extended from dodecahedron-only to all five solids, seven lines, test file only. Clean work against its brief.

Its marginal DETECTION value is approximately zero, and the reason is structural rather than a mistake by the turn.

Measured: hardcode the metric response to the default aniso (2.2), ignoring the caller's. With turn 5's block, 17 assertions fail. With those seven lines deleted, 8 still fail. The bug is caught either way; turn 5 changed how loudly, not whether.

The reason: constellation() does not branch on solid. It maps ONE expression over spec.normals, so the anisotropy code path is identical for a tetrahedron and an icosahedron. An aniso-dependent bug is therefore solid-independent, and one solid swept across the aniso axis already covers it — which is precisely what the dodecahedron sweep was doing. Conversely a solid-SPECIFIC bug (a wrong entry in the normals table) shows up at the default aniso, which the per-solid exactness block already covers. The two existing blocks span the space between them; the new block is their intersection.

THE LESSON, which is about the planner and not this turn: it proposed completing a COVERAGE MATRIX — four solids times four aniso values, an obvious rectangle with a hole in it — by reasoning about the shape of the TEST. Detection value comes from the shape of the CODE: where it branches, and on what. A matrix is only informative along axes the implementation actually distinguishes.

Not worthless, and it should not be reverted: it is insurance against a future change that DOES branch per solid, and a per-solid failure line is more legible than inferring the same from dodecahedron alone. But it is insurance, not detection, and a planner that cannot tell those apart will keep proposing rectangles.

What a planner brief should carry as a result: propose coverage where the implementation BRANCHES. If the code path is shared, one representative case per path is the whole of the coverage, and the rest is decoration.

beads.title: Is the anisotropic squash something a player should FEEL, or something the game should hide?
beads.body:
Every summon so far is exact under a metric with aniso 2.2, so a solid is visibly squashed along Y. I cannot decide from here whether that reads as a deliberate material property of the foam — a thing you learn to exploit — or as a rendering bug the player fights. No gate measures this and either reading is internally consistent, so guessing sets the direction for every mechanic built on top of it.

DO: Open foam, summon a dodecahedron and an icosahedron side by side, and walk around them for a minute at eye level.

WATCH FOR: Whether the squash reads as the world having a grain you could use, or as the shapes being wrong.

SO THAT: If it reads as grain, I propose mechanics that USE the anisotropy — a source that only aligns along Y, a defense that is cheaper across the grain. If it reads as wrong, I propose a compensation pass that renders solids round while keeping the seed geometry exact, and the anisotropy stays a hidden implementation detail.

beads.title: Planning run 2026-08-04T23:17:51Z
beads.body:
A plan seat was staffed because the ready queue was starved. Output: proposals, born proposed, awaiting human promotion.

[turn ? — done] Read the vision, the five already-ready beads, and the full bodies of lp-f25c2f/lp-39d6e7/lp-484b7f to make sure nothing here duplicates them. All three already own the big moves toward playability (atomic multi-insert, real-pocket legality, frame budget) but none of them can land yet without a real pocket, which plant/ does not have — only solids.mjs and the standalone summon inspector exist there. So instead of proposing more geometry (explicitly out of scope per the vision's 'perfecting anything in plant/ that no level uses yet', and per lp-dff7a6/turn-5's finding that another coverage matrix has zero marginal detection value), I proposed two small, independent, inspector-facing tickets: one that gives the existing page a real player-caused fail state using an already-tested primitive (selfCompatible) that nothing currently surfaces, and one that hardens the page's own health check against the exact failure mode this repo keeps rediscovering (green and serving nothing) — because a playable page that silently 404s one of its two script imports is worse than an honestly red one. Filed one ask: whether the new fail state reads as a build constraint or as a broken slider, since that is a taste question no gate can answer and it directly determines whether I keep proposing inspector-scoped playability tickets next turn or switch to holding off until a real pocket exists.

beads.title: The buildability indicator deliberately stops at self-compatibility, not obstacles or the hull
beads.body: lp-39d6e7 is scoped to legality against a real pocket's existing seeds and the indestructible hull, which needs machinery plant/ does not have yet. selfCompatible(con, minSeedGap) only checks a constellation's OWN seeds against each other and is already implemented and unit-tested in solids.mjs — it has just never been surfaced anywhere. beads.title: Does the new self-compatibility fail state read as a build constraint, or as a broken slider?
beads.body:
Proposal 1 above adds a real fail state to the summon inspector — drag the inradius slider down and a solid flips from buildable to not, using the same rule reformPocket enforces elsewhere. But it is surfaced on a raw parameter slider in what is still a library page, not inside anything resembling a level, and I cannot tell from here whether that reads as 'the world has a build constraint you're bumping into' or as 'I turned a dial and got an error message'. This is one layer up from the already-open lp-7c8e6f (whether the anisotropic squash itself should be felt or hidden) — this one is about whether the FAIL STATE built on top of it lands as a mechanic.

DO: Once proposal 1 ships to plant.minomobi.com, pick icosahedron and drag the inradius slider down until the new buildable line flips from green to red.

WATCH FOR: Whether you instinctively try to fix it (raise r back up) before reading why it failed, or read the reason first — that's the difference between it landing as a mechanic and landing as noise.

SO THAT: If it reads as a mechanic, I'll keep proposing small inspector-scoped playability tickets like this one while lp-f25c2f/lp-39d6e7 are still in flight. If it reads as noise, I'll stop proposing anything UI-facing in plant/ next turn and only propose class-d analysis work until a real pocket exists to build an actual level against.

beads.title: Surface self-compatibility as a live buildable/not-buildable verdict in the summon inspector
beads.body: render() in plant/view.js should also return `buildable: selfCompatible(con, 1.5)`, importing selfCompatible from ./solids.mjs (already implemented and unit-tested — see the 'clearance' section of plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs). plant/index.html's #verdict panel gets a second, distinct line: '✓ buildable' (--ok) or '✗ own seeds too close — cannot summon here' (--bad), separate from the existing exactness line — a solid can be geometrically exact and still illegal to place: cube's minimum self-seed-gap is exactly 2r (an already-recorded finding), so at aniso 2.2 anything under r=0.75 already fails, well inside the page's existing r slider range of 0.6-3. This gives the inspector a real, player-caused fail state — drag r down and the verdict flips — which is a small, honest step toward the vision's #1 priority ('something playable, sooner than something perfect') without touching pockets, obstacles or the hull (that is lp-39d6e7's scope, not this one). PATHS (R3): plant/view.js, plant/index.html, plant/test/view.selftest.mjs. Nothing else. GATE (R2): extend plant/test/view.selftest.mjs with known-answer pairs already established in plant/test/solids.selftest.mjs's clearance section — tetrahedron r=1.0 aniso=2.2 buildable; icosahedron r=0.35 aniso=2.2 not buildable; cube r=1.0 aniso=2.2 buildable; octahedron r=0.3 aniso=2.2 not buildable — so the UI verdict can never silently drift from reformPocket's real rule. Do NOT add a full r-by-solid sweep; that is the discouraged coverage-matrix shape the vision and the turn-5 finding both call out. Four known-answer pairs already exercise both outcomes on both an axis-aligned solid (cube) and an off-axis one (icosahedron). R6: three files touched, purely additive, trivially revertable.

beads.title: Harden plant's /health to catch a page that is up but silently broken
beads.body: plant/worker.js's /health only fetches /index.html and reports ok:true if that 200s — but index.html loads solids.mjs and view.js as ES modules at runtime, and if either 404s or is served with the wrong content-type (a real failure mode for a Workers Static Assets deploy), /health stays green while the page renders nothing. worker.js's own comment names exactly this failure ('a worker that is up and serving nothing is the failure this repo keeps rediscovering') but the check does not cover it. Fetch /solids.mjs and /view.js alongside /index.html, report ok only if all three succeed, and include which path failed in the response body so a human debugging a green-but-broken deploy doesn't have to guess. PATHS (R3): plant/worker.js, plant/test/worker.selftest.mjs (new). GATE (R2): a new selftest that imports the worker's default export and calls .fetch(new Request('http://x/health'), { ASSETS: { fetch: mockFn } }) with a mock env.ASSETS.fetch returning canned Response objects for the three paths (all-200, index-only-200, and a middle-path-404 case), asserting the JSON body's ok flag and its failed-path field are each correct — Request/URL/Response are Node 18+ globals so this needs no wrangler runtime. R5: this is the same principle as the repo-wide finding 'Green is not proof: a deploy binds the custom domain or it changed nothing' — applied one layer down, to the page's own liveness check rather than to the deploy log. R6: one file modified (a superset of the current behaviour), one new test file, both trivially revertable.

beads.title: The health probe failed for two minutes after the site was live — one missing space, masked by continue-on-error
beads.body:
plant.minomobi.com went live on its first deploy (run 30959458804) and the health probe reported failure for two minutes after it was already serving. The step was continue-on-error, so the run went green with a masked failure — the worst of both readings.

The cause is one missing space. The worker answers with JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2), which emits:

    "ok": true

and the probe grepped for the string "ok":true with no space. It never could have matched.

What makes this worth recording rather than just fixing is how it read in the log. Attempts 1-7 printed a curl error each (could not resolve host, then HTTP 500 while the certificate issued). Attempts 8-12 printed NO error at all — just "not yet". That silence is the signature: curl had exited 0 and only the grep failed, which means the service was healthy and the check was broken. A health probe that pipes into a matcher has two failure modes that look identical from the outside, and only one of them is the service.

Three things follow:

1. MATCH KEYS, NOT KEY-VALUE PAIRS, unless the formatting is pinned. loop-plant now uses grep -qE with optional whitespace. deploy-loop.yml greps for the key '"beads"' alone and was never exposed to this, by luck rather than design.

2. A CHECK THAT CAN FAIL WHILE THE SERVICE IS HEALTHY IS WORSE THAN NO CHECK, because it teaches you to skip reading it. This one had continue-on-error on top, so it would have gone on silently reporting a false failure indefinitely.

3. THE PROVISIONING SHAPE IS NOW ON RECORD for the next surface created from a routes[] declaration: no DNS at all for ~10s, then Cloudflare error 1104 (HTTP 500) for ~60s while the certificate issues, then correct. Only a first deploy sees it, and it is indistinguishable from a genuine binding failure while it is happening, which is exactly why the tolerance existed and exactly why it had to be removed once it had done its job.
